title: Planted Papers: Dossiers Secrets, MJ-12 and Alternative 3
bigQuestion: What tests can a historian use to tell a planted or invented document from a genuine one?

story.title: Pages No One Remembers
story.kicker: In 1967 a thin typed file about a secret priory enters France's national library, and a legend begins to grow from it.
paragraphs: Picture a cataloguer at the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris in the late 1960s. The national library holds millions of items. Every book and pamphlet printed in France is supposed to be deposited there. Most arrivals are ordinary. Some are strange.

One file is a set of typed and copied pages under the name Henri Lobineau. It is titled Dossiers Secrets, French for secret files. It contains family trees, notes and a list of the grand masters of a hidden order called the Priory of Sion. The list includes famous names such as Leonardo da Vinci and Isaac Newton.

No one on the staff recognizes the author. No scholar has ever mentioned this priory. Yet the file now has a library call number, and anything in the national library carries a quiet kind of authority. Later writers will say they found the secret in the Bibliothèque nationale, as if that alone proved it true.

The file was deposited on 27 April 1967. It was not a lost medieval record. It was a modern invention, planted so that it could be found. In this chapter you will meet three documents like it, one real document that looked just as unlikely, and the tests historians use to tell them apart.
story.think: Why might a forger want a fake document to be found in a famous library rather than simply printed as a pamphlet?

lessons.title: Pages Planted in a Library
lessons.mainIdea: The Dossiers Secrets were typed pages deposited in France's national library in 1967 to make an invented order look historic.
reading: The Dossiers Secrets d'Henri Lobineau entered the Bibliothèque nationale de France on 27 April 1967. A national library is the main library of a country. In France, publishers must send it copies of what they print. That rule is called *legal deposit*, and it means almost anyone can get a printed item onto the library's shelves.

The pages claimed that a secret society called the Priory of Sion had existed since the Middle Ages. They linked it to the Knights Templar and listed a line of grand masters, including Leonardo da Vinci and Isaac Newton. The file offered no medieval originals, no archive references and no way to check its claims.

The trick was about *authority*, the power to be believed because of who or what stands behind a claim. The library's catalog number made the pages look official. But a library records what it receives. It does not certify that the contents are true. The file had been *planted*: placed where it would later be found, so that finding it would seem like discovery. Historians call this a problem of provenance, the known history of where a document came from and who has held it. The Dossiers Secrets had a very short provenance. It began in 1967, with the people who deposited it.

words.d: a rule that publishers must send copies of what they print to a national library
the power to be believed because of who or what stands behind a claim
placed on purpose where it would later be found, to fool the finder
the known history of a document: where it came from and who has held it

look.title: What a Call Number Proves
look.text: A student finds an entry in a national library catalog. It gives a title, an author's name, a year and a shelf number. The student writes in a report: This document is in the national library, so its claims are true.
look.prompt: What does a library catalog entry actually prove about a document? Rewrite the student's sentence so that it claims only what the evidence shows.

check.q: When were the Dossiers Secrets deposited in the Bibliothèque nationale?
check.why: The reading gives 27 April 1967 as the date the file entered the national library.

check.q: What does legal deposit mean?
choices: A rule that publishers send copies of what they print to a national library
A court order to seize a book
A bank account for a library
check.why: Legal deposit is why almost any printed item can enter the national library, whether its claims are true or not.

check.q: Why did being in the library not prove the file was true?
choices: The library had lost the file
The file was written in Latin
A library records what it receives but does not certify its contents
Only books by famous authors are true
check.why: The reading says a library records what it receives and does not certify that the contents are true.

lessons.title: The Makers Confess
lessons.mainIdea: The men behind the Priory of Sion papers, Pierre Plantard and Philippe de Chérisey, later admitted the story was invented.
reading: The Priory of Sion was real in only one sense. In the 1950s a Frenchman named Pierre Plantard registered a small club by that name. It had no connection to the Middle Ages. Plantard, working with his friend Philippe de Chérisey, then produced documents to give the club an ancient past, with Plantard himself as a descendant of old French kings.

The Dossiers Secrets were part of that effort. So were parchments that were said to be medieval. De Chérisey later admitted that he had made the parchments himself. Like the Dossiers, they were *hoaxes*: tricks meant to make people believe something false.

The strongest evidence came from Plantard. In 1993 a French judge was investigating a separate matter in which Plantard's name came up. Under oath, Plantard admitted that his Priory claims had been invented. A *confession* is a person's own statement that they did something. A confession under oath, made to a judge, carries special weight in history as well as in law. So the Priory of Sion is a rare case in which the makers of a hoax told us, on the record, that they made it. Historians did not need to rely on guesswork. The claim that a medieval Priory guided the Templars is shown false.

words.d: a trick meant to make people believe something false
a person's own statement that they did something
after promising formally to tell the truth, as in a court

look.title: Weighing a Confession
look.text: Evidence 1: The Priory's own papers first appear in the 1960s. Evidence 2: No medieval record mentions the Priory. Evidence 3: De Chérisey says he made the parchments. Evidence 4: Plantard admits under oath in 1993 that his Priory claims were invented.
look.prompt: Rank these four pieces of evidence from strongest to weakest. Explain why a sworn confession by the maker might be stronger than the silence of medieval records.

check.q: Who created the Priory of Sion papers?
choices: Pierre Plantard and Philippe de Chérisey
check.why: The reading names Plantard and de Chérisey as the makers of the Priory documents.

check.q: What did Plantard admit under oath in 1993?
choices: That his Priory claims had been invented
That the Priory was founded in 1099
That Newton had been a member
That the library had stolen his papers
check.why: In a 1993 judicial inquiry, Plantard admitted under oath that the Priory claims were invented.

check.q: What is a hoax?
choices: A trick meant to make people believe something false
check.why: A hoax is a deliberate trick. The Priory parchments and Dossiers were hoaxes.

lessons.title: From Hoax to Bestseller
lessons.mainIdea: Popular books turned the Priory hoax into a worldwide legend after its makers' papers had already been planted.
reading: A hoax needs an audience to grow. In 1982 three British authors, Michael Baigent, Richard Leigh and Henry Lincoln, published The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail. They built a large theory on the Priory of Sion papers. The book sold widely and made the Priory famous across the English-speaking world.

In 2003 Dan Brown's novel The Da Vinci Code used the Priory as a central part of its plot. A novel is fiction, and readers know that. But the book's opening pages presented the Priory as real, and many readers took it that way. Tourists began visiting sites linked to the story.

This is how a *legend* can grow from a hoax. A legend is a popular story about the past that is told as if true but cannot be proven. Each retelling cites the one before. After a while, people can point to many books that mention the Priory. None of them leads back to anything older than 1967. Historians call this *circular sourcing*. The sources seem many, but they all rest on the same weak foundation. The test is to follow each claim back, step by step, to its first appearance.

words.d: a popular story about the past told as true but not proven
when many sources seem to agree but all rest on the same original claim
a book that sells a very large number of copies

look.title: How the Priory Story Grew
rows: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail
Plantard admits the story was invented
look.cite: Bibliothèque nationale deposit (1967); Baigent, Leigh and Lincoln (1982); French judicial inquiry (1993); Dan Brown (2003)
look.prompt: The best-known retelling came ten years after the maker's confession. What does that tell you about how corrections travel compared with exciting stories?

check.q: Which 1982 book made the Priory of Sion famous in English?
choices: The Holy Blood and the Holy Grail
check.why: Baigent, Leigh and Lincoln's 1982 book built a large theory on the Priory papers.

check.q: What is circular sourcing?
choices: Checking every source against the original
Many sources that seem to agree but all rest on the same original claim
check.why: Circular sourcing makes a claim look well supported when every source leads back to one weak origin.

check.q: How far back can the Priory claims be traced?
check.why: The reading says none of the retellings leads back to anything older than 1967.

lessons.title: A Roll of Film in the Mail
lessons.mainIdea: The Majestic-12 papers first surfaced in 1984 as undeveloped film mailed anonymously, so they had no traceable history.
reading: In December 1984 a television producer named Jaime Shandera received a package. It held a roll of undeveloped 35 mm film and had a New Mexico postmark. There was no return address. When the film was developed, it showed pages of what looked like a top secret government briefing.

The main paper was labeled as a briefing for President-elect Dwight Eisenhower, dated 18 November 1952. It claimed that in 1947 President Harry Truman had set up a secret committee of twelve officials, called Majestic-12 or MJ-12, to handle a crashed flying saucer. The pages looked official, with stamps, code words and signatures.

The papers became public in 1987. A British author, Timothy Good, published them in May of that year, and American researchers William Moore and Shandera released them in the United States. They caused a sensation among people interested in UFOs. Stamps and signatures are easy to copy onto a page.

Notice the provenance. An *anonymous* source, meaning one with no name, mailed a copy of a copy. There was no original paper to examine, no archive file, and no one who admitted sending it. A document with no traceable history is *unauthenticated*: it has not been shown to be what it claims to be.

words.d: with no name given; from an unknown source
not yet shown to be what it claims to be
a short report that gives a leader key information

look.title: MJ-12 Papers: What Year Is It?
rows: Date typed on the Eisenhower briefing
look.cite: Majestic-12 papers (dated 1952); T. Good (1987); FBI file 'Majestic 12', FBI Records: The Vault
look.prompt: The paper says 1952, but the first time anyone can show it existed is 1984. Which date should a historian use as the start of its known history, and why?

check.q: How did the MJ-12 papers first arrive in 1984?
choices: As undeveloped film mailed with no return address
In a sealed letter from Truman
check.why: Shandera received undeveloped 35 mm film in a package with a New Mexico postmark and no return address.

check.q: What did the papers claim Truman did in 1947?
choices: Set up a secret committee of twelve to handle a crashed saucer
check.why: The papers claimed Truman formed Majestic-12 to handle a crashed flying saucer.

check.q: What does unauthenticated mean?
choices: Not yet shown to be what it claims to be
check.why: An unauthenticated document has not been shown to be genuine; the MJ-12 film had no traceable history.

lessons.title: The FBI Checks With the Air Force
lessons.mainIdea: When the FBI asked, Air Force investigators said no Majestic-12 committee had ever been authorized or formed.
reading: Copies of the MJ-12 papers were marked top secret, so the FBI took notice. A document marked classified might mean a real leak of national secrets. The Bureau's file shows that an agent of the Air Force Office of Special Investigations contacted the FBI's Dallas office on 15 September 1988.

The FBI asked the Air Force to check. On 30 November 1988 the Air Force investigators reported back. No such committee, they said, had ever been authorized or formed. A document said to be *classified* is one officially kept secret. This one, the Air Force concluded, was not a real government document at all.

The file also shows the FBI's own reaction. An FBI official wrote that the document was bogus, and the word bogus was written across a copy in the file. Today the FBI posts this file publicly in its online reading room, called the Vault. It was an FBI verdict on a paper, not a secret.

This record is a good example of a *primary source*, a document created at the time by people directly involved. It lets students watch a government agency test a secret document the way a historian would, by asking the office that would have created it.

words.d: officially kept secret by a government
a document created at the time by people directly involved
a person whose job is to find out the facts about something

look.title: The FBI File, in Summary
look.text: In late 1988 Air Force investigators told the FBI that no Majestic-12 committee had ever been authorized or formed, and an FBI official dismissed the document as bogus.
look.cite: Federal Bureau of Investigation, 'Majestic 12' file (1988), FBI Records: The Vault
look.prompt: Why is asking the office that would have created a document a strong test? What might a believer in MJ-12 say in reply?

check.q: What did Air Force investigators tell the FBI on 30 November 1988?
choices: That no such committee had ever been authorized or formed
That MJ-12 was real but still secret
That the film had been lost
check.why: The FBI file records the Air Force's finding that no Majestic-12 committee was ever authorized or formed.

check.q: What is a primary source?
choices: A modern summary of an event
The most popular book on a topic
A document created at the time by people directly involved
check.why: The FBI's 1988 file is a primary source because it was made at the time by the people investigating.

check.q: Where can the public read the FBI's MJ-12 file today?
choices: In the FBI's online reading room, the Vault
Only in a sealed Air Force vault
check.why: The reading says the FBI posts the file publicly in its online reading room, called the Vault.

lessons.title: The Case For and Against MJ-12
lessons.mainIdea: A few researchers defended the MJ-12 papers, but nearly all investigators judge them forgeries.
reading: Fairness means hearing the defense. The nuclear physicist and UFO researcher Stanton Friedman spent years arguing that the MJ-12 papers might be real. In his 1996 book Top Secret/Majic, he argued that the people named in the papers were real officials and that the details fit their schedules and positions.

Critics answered with several problems. The papers had no provenance: an anonymous roll of film is not an archive. Critics also pointed to features they argued were wrong for real government papers of that time, such as the way dates and markings were written, and a signature they argued had been copied from a genuine letter. And the agency that would have run the committee said it never existed.

Later official reviews found no support either. In March 2024 the Defense Department's All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office, called AARO, reported on the historical record of government UFO programs. It found no evidence that the government had recovered alien technology. The *consensus*, meaning the broad agreement among experts, is that the MJ-12 papers are forgeries. Using real names does not make a document real. Forgers often borrow real people, because real names make a fake easier to believe.

words.d: broad agreement among experts
a person who judges the strengths and weaknesses of a claim or work
seeming reasonable or possible, though not proven

look.title: A Two-Column Ledger
look.text: For the papers: real officials are named; the details fit their jobs; defenders studied them for years. Against the papers: they came on anonymous film; no original exists; the Air Force said the committee was never formed; critics found problems in dates, markings and a signature; a 2024 review found no evidence of recovered alien technology.
look.prompt: Which single point in the against column would be hardest for a defender to answer? Explain why real names in the for column are weak evidence.

check.q: Which researcher argued for years that the MJ-12 papers might be real?
check.why: Stanton Friedman defended the papers, most fully in his 1996 book Top Secret/Majic.

check.q: Why are real officials' names weak evidence that a document is genuine?
choices: Because real officials never wrote memos
Because the FBI removes names from files
Because forgers often borrow real names to make a fake believable
check.why: The reading says forgers use real names because it makes fakes easier to believe.

check.q: What did the AARO report of March 2024 find?
choices: No evidence that the government recovered alien technology
check.why: AARO's review of the historical record found no evidence of recovered alien technology.

lessons.title: Alternative 3 on British TV
lessons.mainIdea: Alternative 3 was a 1977 British television spoof, written and acted as fiction, about a secret plan to leave a dying Earth.
reading: On 20 June 1977, viewers in Britain watched a program from Anglia Television called Alternative 3. It looked like a serious science documentary. Reporters investigated missing scientists and uncovered a secret plan. The world's powers, it claimed, were preparing to move a chosen few to colonies in space, because Earth was becoming unlivable.

The program was a *spoof*, a humorous imitation of a serious form. It was written by the screenwriter David Ambrose and directed by Christopher Miles. The people on screen were actors playing roles. It had been made to air on 1 April, April Fools' Day, but a labor dispute delayed the broadcast until June.

Moving it from April Fools' Day took away its biggest clue. Some viewers believed what they saw. The program ended with credits listing the writer and the cast, the kind of detail real documentaries also have. But people who missed the ending, or heard about it later, had no way to know. The program is an example of a *mockumentary*, a fictional film made in the style of a documentary. Mockumentaries are a real art form. The problem begins when one is cut loose from its context and passed on as fact.

words.d: a humorous imitation of a serious kind of work
a fictional film made in the style of a documentary
the setting and facts around something that help explain what it means

look.title: Missing Clues
look.text: Imagine seeing Alternative 3 in three ways. Viewer A watches it live on April Fools' Day and sees the credits. Viewer B watches it live in June and turns it off before the credits. Viewer C hears about it from a friend years later.
look.prompt: Which viewer is most likely to believe it is real? List the clues each viewer had or lacked.

check.q: Which station broadcast Alternative 3 in 1977?
check.why: Anglia Television broadcast Alternative 3 on 20 June 1977.

check.q: Why did Alternative 3 air in June instead of on 1 April?
choices: The government banned it in April
A labor dispute delayed the broadcast
It was a live news report
check.why: It was made for April Fools' Day, but a labor dispute pushed the broadcast to June.

check.q: What is a mockumentary?
choices: A fictional film made in the style of a documentary
A real documentary about fake news
check.why: Alternative 3 was a mockumentary: fiction made to look like a documentary.

lessons.title: How a Spoof Became a Claim
lessons.mainIdea: After 1977, Alternative 3 was retold in a book and then repeated in conspiracy writing as if it were a real exposé.
reading: In 1978 a writer named Leslie Watkins published a book version of Alternative 3. The book kept the documentary style. On a shelf, it looked like nonfiction. Each new form carried the story further from its first context as an April Fools' spoof. Its readers did not see a cast list.

Over the next years, the story's claims appeared in conspiracy books and talks as evidence of a real secret plan. Bill Cooper, whose 1991 book Behold a Pale Horse this course studies in Unit 17, was one of the writers who repeated Alternative 3 as if it described real events. The show's credits and its writer's name did not travel with the claims.

This is sometimes called *context collapse*. A piece of content is removed from the setting that explained it, and a new audience reads it without the clues. A joke, a novel or a drama can then look like a leak. The claim has not become stronger. It has only lost its label.

The fix is to trace the claim upstream, meaning back toward its first source. Follow Alternative 3 back through the books and talks, and it ends at a television studio, a script and a cast list. That first appearance is its *origin*, and it answers the question.

words.d: when content is removed from the setting that explained it and read by a new audience without clues
the first source or starting point of something
back toward the first source of a claim

look.title: Tracing a Claim Upstream
look.text: Step 4: A post says a secret plan to move the elite into space was exposed on television. Step 3: A conspiracy book repeats the plan as fact. Step 2: A 1978 book tells the story in documentary style. Step 1: A 1977 television spoof with a writer, a director and a cast of actors.
look.prompt: At which step was the fiction label lost? What single question would take a reader from Step 4 back to Step 1?

check.q: Who wrote the 1978 book version of Alternative 3?
check.why: Leslie Watkins wrote the 1978 book version, which kept the documentary style.

check.q: What is context collapse?
choices: When content loses the setting that explained it and reaches a new audience without clues
When a court overturns a verdict
check.why: Context collapse is how Alternative 3 lost its label as a spoof and was read as fact.

check.q: Where does Alternative 3 lead when traced upstream?
choices: To a 1977 television script and cast list
check.why: Tracing it back ends at Anglia's 1977 program, with its writer, director and actors.

lessons.title: Four Tests for Any Document
lessons.mainIdea: Historians test a document by its provenance, its physical materials, its anachronisms, and who gains from it.
reading: Historians use a set of tests on any document that seems too good to be true. The first is provenance. Where did this come from, and who has held it? A letter kept in a family's papers for 150 years, then given to an archive, has strong provenance. A roll of film from an unknown sender has almost none.

The second test is the material itself. Paper, parchment, ink and typewriter type all change over time. Experts can often date a page by what it is made of and how its letters were printed. Checking whether a document is genuine is called *authentication*. The MJ-12 papers could not be tested this way, because only photographs existed.

The third test looks for an *anachronism*, something placed in the wrong time. A word, a title, a date format or an object that did not yet exist can expose a forgery at once. Forgers know the big facts of the past, but they often slip on the small ones.

The fourth test asks who gains. Who benefits if people believe this? Plantard gained a royal family tree. Promoters gained sales and attention. A benefit does not prove a document false, but it tells you where to look harder. Together, these tests turn a feeling of doubt into evidence.

words.d: the process of checking whether a document is genuine
something placed in a time where it does not belong
a reason a person has for doing something

look.title: Match the Test
look.text: Clue 1: The document arrived by anonymous mail. Clue 2: The paper contains a kind of fiber first made decades after the date on the page. Clue 3: A letter dated 1850 mentions a telephone call. Clue 4: The document names its finder as the heir to a lost throne.
look.prompt: Match each clue to one of the four tests: provenance, material, anachronism, or who gains. Which clue alone would be enough to prove a forgery?

check.q: What does the provenance test ask?
choices: Where the document came from and who has held it
check.why: Provenance is a document's known history of origin and custody.

check.q: Why could the MJ-12 papers not pass the material test?
choices: Only photographs existed, not original paper
They were too old to test
check.why: The reading says only photographs existed, so the paper and ink could not be examined.

check.q: A letter dated 1850 mentions a telephone call. Which test does this fail?
check.why: A telephone in an 1850 letter is something placed in a time before it existed, an anachronism.

lessons.title: A Real Find: The Chinon Parchment
lessons.mainIdea: The Chinon Parchment, found in the Vatican archives in 2001, passes the tests, but it proves less than some headlines claimed.
reading: Not every surprising document is fake. In September 2001 an Italian scholar, Barbara Frale, was working in the Vatican archives. She identified a parchment that had been misfiled for centuries. A catalog entry from 1628 had mentioned it, but too vaguely for anyone to find it. It recorded questioning of the Knights Templar at Chinon, in France.

The parchment is dated 17 to 20 August 1308. It records that three cardinals, sent by Pope Clement V, questioned the Templar Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, and other leaders. The cardinals *absolved* them, meaning they formally forgave them of sin and restored them to the Church's sacraments.

Compare its tests with the planted papers. Its provenance is strong: it sat in the pope's own archive for about seven centuries. Its material is a medieval parchment. Its contents fit other records of the Templar trials. It gave no one a throne or a fortune. In 2007 the Vatican published a facsimile, a careful exact copy, of the trial documents.

But a genuine document can still be overstated. Some headlines said the pope had declared the Templars innocent. The parchment does not say that. It did not end the case. The order was still suppressed in 1312, and Molay was burned in 1314. Reading carefully means claiming only what the *document* shows.

words.d: formally forgiven of sin by church authority
a careful, exact copy of a document
a written or printed record that gives information or evidence
put in the wrong place in a set of records

look.title: The Chinon Parchment Through Time
look.cite: Chinon Parchment, Vatican Apostolic Archive; Processus contra Templarios (Vatican, 2007)
look.prompt: The Dossiers Secrets have a known history starting in 1967. How long is the Chinon Parchment's known history? How does that difference affect how much we trust each one?

check.q: Who identified the Chinon Parchment in 2001?
check.why: Barbara Frale identified the misfiled parchment in the Vatican archives in September 2001.

check.q: What does the parchment record the cardinals doing in 1308?
choices: Absolving Molay and other Templar leaders
check.why: The cardinals absolved the leaders, forgiving them of sin and restoring them to the sacraments.

check.q: Why is the claim that the parchment proves the Templars innocent an overstatement?
choices: Because the parchment is a forgery
Because Frale later admitted making it
Because it records absolution but did not end the case; the order was still suppressed in 1312
Because it was found in a Paris library
check.why: The parchment is genuine, but it records forgiveness, not a verdict of innocence, and the order was still suppressed.

lessons.title: Try It Yourself
lessons.mainIdea: Students can apply the four tests to a practice document and explain their verdict with evidence.
reading: Now it is your turn to be the historian. Below is a practice document. It is invented for this lesson, so you can test it without harm. Your job is not to guess. Your job is to find evidence and explain it. Take your time; careful work matters more than speed. Read the whole document once before you begin testing it.

Work through the tests in order. For provenance, ask who found it and how it reached them. For material, ask what it is written on and how. For anachronism, read every date, word and object slowly. For who gains, ask who benefits if people believe it. Write one sentence of evidence for each test.

Then reach a *verdict*, a judgment based on evidence. Historians use three honest labels. A document can be authenticated, meaning shown to be genuine. It can be shown false, meaning evidence proves it is not what it claims. Or it can be *unverified*, meaning there is not yet enough evidence either way. Remember the lesson of Chinon. A strange document is not automatically fake, and a real document is not automatically proof of everything people claim. Good judgment stays close to the evidence, in both directions.

words.d: a judgment reached after weighing the evidence
not yet checked or proven either way
shown by evidence to be genuine

look.title: Practice Document (Invented for This Lesson)
look.text: A typed page, found last month in an attic box by a man selling a book about his family. It reads: Secret Order of the Lantern, minutes of 4 July 1846. Members present: twelve. Our grand master, an ancestor of the finder, reports that the order's gold is hidden near the river. Send replies to our lodge, ZIP code 60601.
look.prompt: Apply all four tests. ZIP codes began in the United States in 1963. What is your verdict, and which piece of evidence decides it?

check.q: In the practice document, which detail is an anachronism?
choices: A ZIP code in a document dated 1846
check.why: ZIP codes began in 1963, so one could not appear in minutes dated 1846.

check.q: Which test does the finder's book about his family raise?
check.why: The finder benefits if people believe his ancestor led a secret order, so the who-gains test applies.

check.q: What does unverified mean as a verdict?
choices: Not yet enough evidence either way
check.why: Unverified means the evidence does not yet settle the question in either direction.

review.q: What made the Dossiers Secrets seem official?
choices: They had a call number in France's national library
review.why: Being deposited in the Bibliothèque nationale gave them a catalog number and borrowed authority.

review.q: Which piece of evidence most directly shows the Priory of Sion story was invented?
choices: Its list of famous grand masters
Tourist visits to sites in the story
review.why: The maker's own sworn confession is direct evidence that the Priory claims were invented.

review.q: Why did the MJ-12 papers have weak provenance?
choices: They arrived as anonymous film with no original paper
They were printed in a newspaper
review.why: An anonymous roll of film is a copy of a copy, with no traceable history.

review.q: What did Air Force investigators report to the FBI about Majestic-12?
choices: That no such committee had ever been authorized or formed
review.why: The FBI file records the Air Force's finding that no such committee ever existed.

choices: A French forgery in a library
A 1977 television spoof with a writer, director and actors
review.why: Anglia Television made it as a spoof documentary, first meant for April Fools' Day.

review.q: A letter dated 1790 mentions a railroad station. Which test does it fail?
review.why: A railroad station in 1790 is something placed in a time before it existed.

review.q: How does the Chinon Parchment differ from the planted papers?
choices: It was first a TV spoof
It has strong provenance in the Vatican archive for about seven centuries
review.why: The parchment stayed in the pope's own archive and fits other trial records.

review.q: Which statement about the Chinon Parchment is accurate?
choices: It proves the pope declared the Templars innocent
It is a forgery by Plantard
It was found by the FBI
It records that cardinals absolved the Templar leaders in 1308, though the order was still suppressed
review.why: It records absolution, not a verdict of innocence, and the order was suppressed in 1312.
